title: The endocrine system
note: Hormones are amines, peptides and proteins, or steroids. Lipid-soluble hormones (steroids and thyroid hormone) enter cells and bind intracellular receptors that change gene transcription; water-soluble hormones bind surface receptors and act through second messengers such as cAMP. Most hormone levels are held in range by negative feedback.

read.title: A thermostat made of hormones
text: Most hormones are kept in range the way a thermostat keeps a room warm: by negative feedback. The thyroid shows the pattern clearly. When thyroid hormone in the blood falls, the hypothalamus releases thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH). TRH travels a very short route, through the hypophyseal portal veins, to the anterior pituitary, which answers by secreting thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).

TSH reaches the thyroid through the general circulation. There, follicle cells take up iodide and attach it to thyroglobulin stored in the colloid, and the gland releases mostly T4 with a smaller amount of T3. Many tissues convert T4 to the more potent T3, which enters cells, binds receptors in the nucleus, and raises the basal metabolic rate.

As thyroid hormone levels climb, they inhibit both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, so TRH and TSH fall and the thyroid slows down. The final product switches off the signals that called for it.

The same three-tier design, hypothalamus to pituitary to target gland, controls cortisol through CRH and ACTH and the sex steroids through GnRH, FSH, and LH. Some hormones skip the tiers entirely. Insulin and glucagon respond directly to the blood glucose they regulate, and parathyroid hormone responds directly to blood calcium.
